title: Where I Find the Time: Exercise Books
author: Lee Wheeler
summary: Lee Wheeler answers the question of where he finds time for spaced retrieval and atomised teaching by auditing where lesson minutes actually go. Borrowing Descartes' method, he questions every part of an ordinary lesson and asks whether it helps learning. His clearest example is the exercise book: handing out, dating, titling, marking margins and packing away cost seven to eleven minutes in a well-drilled class, which he estimates at about a hundred hours of maths over five years of secondary school. He then tests the usual arguments for books, that they show learning, support revision, build pride or give the lesson a title, and finds each wanting. His classes use retrieval worksheets and mini whiteboards, with a fixed lesson structure and sheets stored by date, which he argues gives a better record of what pupils can do weeks later. He admits the cost that tracking one pupil takes about ten minutes of sorting.
points: Wheeler found time by auditing each part of a lesson and asking whether it justified its place, the method he borrows from Descartes.
He estimates exercise-book routines cost seven to eleven minutes per lesson even in the best case, about a hundred hours of maths across five years.
He rejects common reasons for books, arguing they do not show learning, are rarely used for revision, and bring constant enforcement disputes over presentation.
His lessons run on retrieval worksheets and mini whiteboards in a predictable structure, which he says helps pupils with SEND and frees attention for the maths.
Keeping every sheet by date gives independent evidence of spaced retrieval, at the cost of ten minutes when someone wants one pupil's journey.
quotes: A minute of rest isn’t wasted just because it looks empty. And a lot of minutes that look busy are wasted. What matters is what a minute is doing.
Take an ordinary lesson, go through it bit by bit, and ask what actually happened in each part and whether it did anything for learning.
But the easiest win by a long way is just to leave out the things that can’t justify being let back in. And the clearest example I know is the exercise book.
In an hour’s lesson that’s an eighth to a fifth of the lesson, every lesson. At four lessons a week for a year it’s around twenty hours per class, which is about five weeks of maths.
even a perfect book doesn’t show the learning. There is a big difference between what is written in a book and what has actually been learned.

How many book looks have you been in where all anyone says is that the title isn’t underlined or the green pen hasn’t been used. How often do you hear a meaningful discussion about understanding or retention.
Because the transitions are the same every lesson, nobody spends time or attention on them, and that leaves more time and more thinking for the maths.
It’s a cost paid now and then by the one person who wants to look, instead of a cost paid every lesson by thirty kids. I’ll take that trade every time.
